title: The Dog in the Manger
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Dog was lying in a Manger on the hay which had been put there for the cattle, and when they came and tried to eat, he growled and snapped at them and wouldn't let them get at their food. "What a selfish beast," said one of them to his companions; "he can't eat himself and yet he won't let those eat who can."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where is the Dog lying?
options: Beside the cattle's water trough
Under a nearby tree
In a Manger on the hay
Inside the farmhouse

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who was the hay in the Manger meant for?
options: The cattle
The Dog himself
The farmer's horses
A different farm entirely

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Dog do when the cattle try to eat?
options: He shares the hay willingly
He runs away and hides
He barks to call the farmer
He growls and snaps at them

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the cattle call the Dog?
options: A clever trickster
A selfish beast
A dangerous animal
A lazy creature

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the cattle point out about the Dog and the hay?
options: He eats it slowly to make it last longer
He hides it from the other dogs on the farm
He can't eat it himself, yet won't let those who can eat it
He only eats it when no one is watching

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the cattle's comment call the Dog's behavior senseless rather than merely unkind?
options: He denies others something he has no actual use for himself
He is punished for his actions by the farmer
He eventually realizes his mistake and shares the hay
He is unaware that hay is not food for dogs

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "Manger" refer to in the passage?
options: A small barn for storing tools
A fenced field for grazing
A wooden cart for hauling hay
A feeding trough for animals

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "companions" mean in "said one of them to his companions"?
options: Strangers passing by
Fellow members of the same group
The Dog's owners
Workers on the farm

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "selfish" mean in "What a selfish beast"?
options: Extremely hungry and desperate
Confused about what is happening
Concerned only with one's own wants, without regard for others
Frightened of the surrounding cattle

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Denying others a benefit you cannot use yourself is a pointless kind of selfishness
Dogs should never be allowed near cattle feed
Cattle are wiser than dogs about sharing resources
Selfishness always leads to eventual punishment

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what were the cattle trying to do?
options: Escape from their pen
Find fresh water nearby
Sleep in the Manger themselves
Eat the hay in the Manger

questions.prompt: According to the passage, who speaks the complaint about the Dog?
options: The farmer who owns the Manger
One of the cattle, to his companions
Another dog passing by
A bird watching from a nearby tree

questions.prompt: According to the passage, does the Dog actually eat the hay himself?
options: Yes, he eats a small amount of it
Yes, he eats all of it eventually
No, the passage says he can't eat it himself
The passage does not say either way

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the cattle feel their complaint is especially justified?
options: The Dog gains nothing from keeping them away, making his behavior pure spite
The Dog has promised to share the hay later
The cattle believe the hay actually belongs to the Dog
The cattle are the ones who put the hay there originally

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Dog's growling and snapping suggest about his reason for guarding the hay?
options: It is meant to protect the hay from spoiling
It is meant to train the cattle to be more careful
It is meant to warn the cattle of a hidden danger
It seems driven by simple possessiveness rather than any real need

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does it mean that the Dog "snapped at" the cattle?
options: He spoke sharply in words to them
He tried to bite at them threateningly
He jumped quickly away from them
He offered them a small portion of hay

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Dog shares the Manger's hay evenly with the cattle
A Dog eats all the hay before the cattle arrive
A Dog refuses to let cattle eat hay he himself has no use for, and they call him selfish for it
The cattle drive the Dog away from the Manger
